stem: A multiparous client gives birth 2 hours 45 minutes after regular contractions begin. Cervical dilation and fetal descent progress rapidly, but no contraction-frequency data are documented. Which labor pattern best describes this course?
rationale: NCBI Bookshelf describes precipitous labor as extremely rapid labor and delivery, usually less than 3 hours from the start of contractions to birth; NCBI MedGen likewise defines it as fetal expulsion in less than 3 hours after regular contractions begin. A 2-hour-45-minute labor therefore meets this definition. Tachysystole is a contraction-frequency diagnosis and cannot be inferred from total labor duration alone, while arrest or prolonged labor requires inadequate or delayed progress rather than rapid dilation, descent, and birth.
educational_objective: Identify precipitous labor when birth occurs less than 3 hours after regular contractions begin and distinguish this duration-based pattern from contraction-frequency or labor-arrest disorders.
source_organization: National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI), National Library of Medicine
source_document_title: Nursing Health Promotion — Labor & Delivery Care; MedGen — Precipitous labor (C0473472)
source_locator: NCBI Bookshelf chapter 'Labor & Delivery Care' → 'Precipitous Labor'; MedGen UID 633244 → Definition.
source_claim_supported: NCBI defines precipitous labor as extremely rapid labor and delivery, usually less than 3 hours from onset of contractions to birth; MedGen specifies less than 3 hours from commencement of regular contractions.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)

source_original.stem: A multiparous client gives birth 2 hours 45 minutes after regular contractions begin. Cervical dilation and fetal descent progress rapidly, but no contraction-frequency data are documented. Which labor pattern best describes this course?
source_original.rationale: NCBI Bookshelf's current Open RN labor-and-delivery chapter defines precipitous labor as labor and delivery that are extremely rapid, usually less than 3 hours from the start of contractions to birth, so option A fits. Option B cannot be established from total labor duration because tachysystole is defined by contraction frequency over time. Option C is the opposite pattern: an arrest disorder requires absent cervical progress, not rapid dilation followed by birth. Option D is incorrect because multiparity may shorten labor but does not remove a sub-3-hour course from the precipitous-labor definition.
source_original.source_detail: NCBI MedGen, Precipitous labor, Concept ID C0473472 / MedGen UID 633244 — Definition: expulsion of fetus in less than 3 hours from commencement of regular contractions. correction_summary: Retained the sub-3-hour construct and key. Replaced the narrower 'prolonged latent phase' distractor with the broader prolonged-labor comparator and anchored the definition to the current NCBI Bookshelf labor chapter plus MedGen. Recalibrated difficulty from hard to medium because the item hinges on one directly defined duration threshold.

audit_findings.exact_locator: The NCBI Bookshelf 'Precipitous Labor' subsection and MedGen definition directly support the <3-hour threshold.
audit_findings.claim_audit: The 2-hour-45-minute value is directly compared with a sourced threshold; no unsupported contraction-frequency threshold is introduced.

distractor_audit.B: Cannot be diagnosed without contraction-frequency data.
distractor_audit.C: Contradicted by rapid cervical progress and birth.
distractor_audit.D: Contradicted by the very short total labor duration.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A is established by the documented duration/progression data.
